entries.claim: Division of polynomials can be calculated using long division, similar to integers.
entries.quote: Division of polynomials can be calculated using long division
entries.note: Exact match in the Point! box

entries.claim: In problems where you 'treat as a polynomial in x', treat other variables as constants.
entries.note: Exact match in the Point! box

entries.claim: Common Mistakes: errors in subtraction, often after multiplication, especially forgetting to change signs or combine like terms properly. Partial multiplication: multiplying only by the leading term of the divisor instead of the entire divisor.
entries.quote: Errors in subtraction: Mistakes often happen when subtracting after multiplication
entries.note: The Common Mistakes box lists both errors. It says subtraction errors often happen after multiplication, especially forgetting to change signs or combine like terms. It also lists partial multiplication, meaning multiplying only by the leading term of the divisor instead of the entire divisor. The claim condenses this wording but adds nothing.
entries.first_note: Content is present but the claim restructures and reorders the text differently from how it appears in the Common Mistakes box

entries.claim: If a polynomial A is divided by a polynomial B, giving quotient Q and remainder R, then A = B × Q + R.
entries.quote: If a polynomial A is divided by a polynomial B, yielding a quotient Q and a remainder R

entries.claim: In problems where the quotient and the remainder are given, substitute the known expressions into A = BQ + R.
entries.quote: In problems where the quotient and the remainder are given, substitute

entries.claim: Stopping too early: ending the division before reaching a remainder of lower degree than the divisor.
entries.quote: Stopping too early: Ending the division before reaching a remainder

entries.claim: Confusing quotient and remainder: thinking the remainder must always be zero, while in fact it can be a term (or more) of lower degree than the divisor.
entries.quote: Confusing quotient and remainder: Thinking the remainder must always be zero
